holidays.name: New Beer's Eve
holidays.description: Raise a glass to the night before beer came back! This unofficial party day celebrates the eve of the end of Prohibition, when thirsty Americans counted down the hours until a legal brew was within reach.
holidays.origin: It commemorates April 6, 1933, the day before the Cullen-Harrison Act took effect and made low-alcohol beer legal again in the United States after years of Prohibition.
holidays.funFact: When the law took effect at midnight, breweries rushed trucks of beer out, and crowds gathered to celebrate. Anheuser-Busch even sent a team of Clydesdales to deliver beer to the White House.

holidays.name: National Caramel Popcorn Day
holidays.description: A day to celebrate the sweet, sticky, crunchy snack that turns a movie night into a candy-coated adventure. Grab a bowl, and maybe some napkins.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial snack observance of unclear origin, celebrated each year on April 6.
holidays.funFact: Caramel corn became a household name through Cracker Jack, which debuted in the 1890s and was famously mentioned in the 1908 baseball song 'Take Me Out to the Ball Game.'

holidays.name: Tartan Day
holidays.description: A celebration of Scottish heritage in which people show off their plaids, kilts and bagpipe skills. Tartan patterns take center stage, from clan-specific designs to fashion statements.
holidays.origin: Tartan Day began in Canada in the 1980s and later spread to the United States and other countries. April 6 was chosen because it is the date of the 1320 Declaration of Arbroath, Scotland's famous statement of independence.
holidays.funFact: Each tartan pattern can be tied to a specific Scottish clan, district, or organization, and New York City hosts a big Tartan Day Parade with thousands of pipers.
